title: Organic superconductors: charge-transfer salts, Mott physics and pairing probes
summary: Compare molecular salts through pressure, cooling history, nodal transport and spin response, while separating superconducting transitions from Mott endpoints and probe conditions.

review.scope: Selected Lefebvre phase/probe, Izawa angular-transport, Kagawa Mott-scaling and Shinagawa spin-response passages, plus scoped discovery metadata and prior B9 checks.
limitations: Complete scientific acceptance, final-version comparisons and raw-data reproduction remain open.
Jerome1980 original text is inaccessible here; Kini1990 is title/metadata-only; Lee2001/2002 is abstract-only.
Kagawa full methods/supplement and Papanikolaou theoretical proof remain outside this check.
Synthetic algebra does not establish a unique gap symmetry, universality class or common mechanism across molecular families.

claims.statement: Organic charge-transfer salts provide distinct low-dimensional settings for superconductivity. The Bechgaard salts (TMTSF)₂X have strongly anisotropic electronic motion; the κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂X family has conducting molecular layers and is widely studied near a pressure-controlled Mott transition. The anion, molecular packing, sample history and field direction are part of the material identity. A pairing assignment for one salt or field regime is not a classification of the entire family.
claims.conditions: Salt, packing, pressure, cooling history, field direction, probe and transition criterion are distinct. Mott endpoints, anion ordering and probe temperatures are not superconducting Tc.
claims.verificationScope: Selected original passages and bounded observable algebra; abstract-only and access limits remain explicit. Full scientific acceptance is open.

claims.statement: The 1980 Jérome report identifies superconductivity in (TMTSF)₂PF₆. Its bibliographic identity is checked here, while the original experimental text remains an access gap. For κ-Br, the 1990 Kini paper explicitly distinguishes an inductive onset of 11.6 K from a resistive onset of 12.5 K in its title. Those criteria should survive quotation and database export. Its original publication is July 1990; the publisher's 2002 online date does not move the discovery into a later decade.

claims.statement: Izawa's rotating-field thermal-conductivity analysis separates $\kappa(\theta)=C_0+C_2\cos(2\theta)+C_4\cos(4\theta)$, where the angle is between the heat current and the in-plane field. The large twofold term has a substantial phonon-scattering contribution, whereas the low-temperature fourfold term is interpreted through nodal quasiparticles. An independent synthetic harmonic-recovery check confirms the decomposition algebra, not the original fit or the inferred gap symmetry. A 45° rotation reverses the sign of the fourfold basis function, so node labels require a stated crystallographic convention.

claims.statement: The normal-state anisotropic shift used by Shinagawa is $K=K_{\mathrm{iso}}+K_{\mathrm{ax}}(3\cos^2\theta-1)$, with $K_{\mathrm{iso}}=3.9\times10^{-4}$ and $K_{\mathrm{ax}}=10.5\times10^{-4}$. Substitution gives 2,490 ppm at 0° and −660 ppm at 90°. These are signed model contributions, not directly the observed superconducting change. Reducing the spin contribution can move resonance shifts in opposite directions for two orientations. Hyperfine calibration, chemical shifts, screening fields and pulse heating must therefore accompany a spin-pairing inference.

claims.statement: Kagawa's transport analysis found approximate exponents $(\delta,\beta,\gamma)=(2,1,1)$, satisfying $\delta=1+\gamma/\beta$. Checking that identity does not independently validate a universality class. The analysis maps conductance onto an order parameter and treats pressure/temperature mixing within stated approximations; it excludes the closest region to the endpoint because of calibration and sample limitations. A later theoretical treatment shows how conductivity can couple to singular quantities other than the thermodynamic order parameter. Transport exponents and thermodynamic exponents must not be equated automatically.

claims.statement: Lefebvre's κ-Cl phase diagram combines proton NMR with AC susceptibility under helium-gas pressure. NMR uses a 0.5 T field perpendicular to the layers; susceptibility uses an approximately 0.05 Oe oscillating field parallel to them, without a static field. Slow pressure and temperature sweeps, restricted to helium's fluid region, resolve hysteresis and changing phase fractions. The reported meeting region near 282 bar and 13.1 K is not evidence that antiferromagnetism and superconductivity occupy every microscopic volume together: the paper explicitly discusses inhomogeneous coexistence.

claims.statement: In the separate κ-Cl conductance experiment, a critical endpoint occurs near 39.7 ± 0.1 K and 24.8 ± 0.1 MPa. Here the paper's symbol Tc denotes the Mott endpoint, not a superconducting transition. Four-probe measurements, helium pressure sweeps near 3 MPa per hour and a current-independence check over two orders of magnitude underpin this assignment. The endpoint pressure is 0.0248 GPa; confusing MPa with GPa would introduce a factor of one thousand.

claims.statement: Izawa studies κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂Cu(NCS)₂ with a reported resistive transition near 10.4 K. Heat flows along the b axis, with in-plane field alignment better than 0.01°. At 2 T the fourfold component becomes visible around 0.52 and 0.43 K, at approximately 0.2% of the normal-state total conductivity. These low temperatures are probe conditions, not additional transition temperatures. Extracting such a small electronic modulation requires separating phonons, vortex scattering and the field/temperature regime; the sign cannot be interpreted without that model.

claims.statement: For (TMTSF)₂ClO₄, Shinagawa's samples were cooled at 7 mK per minute through anion ordering near 24 K and showed resistive/rf onset near 1.4 K. NMR pulses with tip angles below 3° were checked for heating using simultaneous resistance measurements. Low-field shifts support reduced spin susceptibility, while relaxation near 100 mK changes sharply around 15 kOe. That crossover field is neither a superconducting temperature nor, by itself, a unique identification of an FFLO or triplet state.

claims.statement: The earlier Lee result concerns a different salt, (TMTSF)₂PF₆, at 7 kbar with field along the conducting a axis; its abstract reports little Knight-shift change and argues for triplet pairing. The later ClO₄ study finds a low-field singlet-compatible response and leaves its high-field state unresolved. These are condition-specific observations. High upper critical fields, unchanged shifts in one regime or proximity to spin-density-wave order cannot alone establish family-wide p-wave superconductivity.

claims.statement: For κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂Cu₂(CN)₃, absence of magnetic ordering down to 32 mK motivated a spin-liquid interpretation, while pressure studies found a neighboring superconducting region. Subsequent spin-gap work supports a valence-bond interpretation but does not uniquely exclude a gapped chiral spin liquid. Mounting strain and microcracks complicate comparison with a nominally hydrostatic experiment. Neither an exchange scale nor a spin-gap anomaly should become a superconducting Tc record.

claims.statement: Compare pressure, chemical substitution and strain through measured phase diagrams rather than treating them as interchangeable tuning knobs. Report the exact salt, cooling protocol, pressure medium, field orientation and transition criterion before comparing performance. A useful next measurement should distinguish competing explanations—for example by combining bulk thermodynamics, low-heating spin probes and controlled-disorder studies on the same specimen. A nearby Mott state constrains a mechanism without identifying it uniquely.

claims.statement: Molecular superconductors also provide a warning against copying symmetry names between coordinate systems. The κ-NCS thermal-conductivity paper discusses nodal directions relative to b and c as well as a rotated convention. Preserve those directions and the observable itself when comparing with theories. Fullerides belong to a separate molecular family with different orbital degeneracy and vibronic physics; the shared word “organic” does not make their pairing evidence interchangeable.
